8.old: There is no legal definition of a penthouse in BC. On MLS®, it's a style the listing agent picks for a unit, usually on the top floor of an apartment building. Some penthouses take up a whole floor. Others share the top floor with a few other units. Many have higher ceilings, a larger deck or a private roof deck, but none of that is guaranteed by the name.
8.new: A penthouse has no legal definition in BC. On MLS®, the listing agent picks it as a style for a unit, normally one at the top of an apartment building. A penthouse may fill an entire floor, or it may sit on the top floor alongside a few other units. Some have a private roof deck, a larger deck or higher ceilings, though the name promises none of these.

9.old: Because the tag is chosen by the agent, a few top-floor units never get it, and a few listings use "PH" in the unit number without the tag. When you're looking, I check the tag, the floor and the unit number together, so a good unit doesn't slip past you.
9.new: Because the agent chooses the tag, some top-floor units never get it, while a few listings have PH in the unit number but lack the tag. So that a good unit doesn't slip past you, I weigh the floor, the unit number and the tag as a set.

17.old: Every penthouse is a strata lot, so you're buying into a strata corporation under BC's Strata Property Act. A top-floor unit raises a few questions that lower floors don't.
17.new: Because a penthouse is a strata lot, the strata corporation and BC's Strata Property Act both apply to you. A top-floor unit raises some extra questions that lower floors don't.

19.old: A roof deck is often limited common property: common property set aside for one unit's use, not part of the unit itself. The strata plan and bylaws show who can use it, what you can put on it and who pays for upkeep.
19.new: Roof decks are frequently limited common property, which is common property reserved for a single unit's use rather than being part of the unit. The strata plan and bylaws set out who may use it, which items it can hold and who pays to maintain it.

23.old: Fees are usually based on unit entitlement, set out on the strata plan. A larger unit often has a higher entitlement and a higher monthly fee. The Form B Information Certificate shows the exact fee, any special levies and the bylaws in force.
23.new: The Form B Information Certificate lists the exact monthly fee, any special levies and which bylaws are in force. Unit entitlement, which appears on the strata plan, normally drives the fees, and bigger units tend to hold more entitlement, which means a higher monthly fee.

28.old: A penthouse is a top-floor unit that the listing agent has tagged with the Penthouse style. There is no legal definition, so confirm the floor and layout yourself.
28.new: A penthouse is, in practice, a top-floor unit that its listing agent gave the Penthouse style. The term has no legal definition, so check the floor and layout for yourself.

34.old: Not always. A roof deck is often limited common property, set aside for one unit. The strata plan and bylaws show who uses it and who pays for upkeep.
34.new: Often not. A lot of roof decks are limited common property reserved for one unit, and the strata plan and bylaws state who uses it and who covers upkeep.

36.old: Strata fees are usually based on unit entitlement. A larger unit often has a higher entitlement, so check the Form B for the exact monthly amount.
36.new: Fees generally follow unit entitlement, so a bigger unit often carries more entitlement and a higher fee. The Form B states the exact monthly amount.

38.old: The Form B Information Certificate, the bylaws and rules, recent minutes, the depreciation report and the financial statements. Look for roof, membrane and elevator items.
38.new: Documents to review: the bylaws and rules, recent minutes, the financial statements, the depreciation report and the Form B Information Certificate. Roof, membrane and elevator items are what to look for.

40.old: Unit numbers like PH1 help, but not every penthouse uses them and not every top-floor unit is tagged. I check the tag, the floor and the unit number together.
40.new: A unit number such as PH1 is a useful clue, yet some penthouses don't use one and some top-floor units aren't tagged. In each case I weigh the floor, the tag and the unit number against each other.
